newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea prepares to head back to work.
newsitem.headline: South Korea prepares to head back to work.

text.p: For the first time since a controversial labour bill was rammed through parliament more than three weeks ago, South Korean factories on Sunday geared up for normal work without strikes.
But the fate of seven fugitive unionists sheltering from arrest in Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral was unresolved even after they backed away from indefinite stoppages.

In a major shift, the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions is now focusing on trying to revise the new law after insisting it be scrapped. The law makes it easier for firms to sack workers and replace strikers.
But the government shows no signs of backing down, and another union leader was arrested on Saturday, bringing to five the number picked up in recent days.
With a tight security net still in place around the cathedral, and regular clashes between workers and riot police in the streets, the situation remained volatile.
On Saturday confederation head Kwon Young-kil said union members would limit strikes to one day each week on Wednesdays.
Several international labour leaders were due to arrive on Sunday to replace four others who left the country last Thursday after being threatened with deportation.
A 10-member mission headed by Bill Jordon, who heads the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, is on its way to monitor treatment of union leaders.
South Korea's top immigration official has said the delegation would be allowed in but warned it would be expelled if members joined strike-related protests.
Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, the nation's largest car maker, reopened on Saturday.
Other key factories in the export sector have operated normally for several days.
Stoppages since the December 26 passage of the law have caused production losses of at least 2.6 trillion won ($3.1 billion) and $467 million in lost exports.
The latest union leader to be arrested was seized in the southeastern city of Ulsan, home of the Hyundai Group, which has been at the forefront of the strikes.

President Kim Young-sam has put his waning popularity on the line by refusing to revise or scrap the law, arguing that labour reform is crucial to trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.
Many South Koreans support a more flexible labour market, but resent the way the legislation was adopted with no debate in a half-empty chamber of ruling party deputies at dawn.

In a nod to popular concerns, Kim's top troubleshooter during the strikes, the chairman of the ruling New Korea Party Lee Hong-koo, last week expressed "humble regret" for the government's parliamentary tactics.
Lee called for dialogue and compromise.

Yet he too ruled out revising the law, and slapped down an offer by confederation head Kwon Young-kil to appear together in a live television debate. Lee had challenged union leaders to face off with ruling party officials in a studio.

Any decision to storm the cathedral and drag out the seven unionists camped out in a ramshackle tent would spark a political storm in a country where more than a quarter of the population are practising Christians.
The influential head of the Roman Catholic church, Cardinal Stephen Kim, appealed to both sides for a peacefully solution afer a private meeting last week with the president.
